title: SOC Operations
description: Master foundational SOC operational procedures: architecture, alerts vs events, alert triage, false positive elimination, severity classification, tiered escalation, and audit-grade documentation.

topics.title: SOC Architecture
topics.description: Understand the three pillars (People, Process, Technology) and how telemetry flows through ingestion pipelines.

content.text: A Security Operations Center (SOC) is built on three interdependent pillars: People, Process, and Technology. Skilled analysts (People) execute repeatable Standard Operating Procedures (Process) using advanced monitoring platforms (Technology) to defend the enterprise.
content.subtitle: The Three Foundational Pillars of Modern Security Operations

techBox.title: The Three SOC Pillars
techBox.content:
• People: Tier 1 (Triage), Tier 2 (Incident Response), Tier 3 (Threat Hunting / Malware Analysis), SOC Lead, CISO
• Process: Standard Operating Procedures (SOPs), Triage Playbooks, Escalation Matrices, SLA Standards
• Technology: SIEM (Correlation), EDR (Endpoint Telemetry), NDR (Network Inspection), SOAR (Automation), Firewalls

knowMore.title: NIST SP 800-61 Incident Handling Architecture
knowMore.content: NIST emphasizes that buying security tools without disciplined processes and trained staff creates blind spots and alert fatigue.

units.title: Topic 2: SOC Data Flow & Ingestion Pipeline

content.text: Telemetry flows across five sequential stages: Event Generation on endpoints and network devices, Forwarding via secure TLS shippers, Centralized Parsing and Normalization into standard schemas (CIM/OSSEM), Correlation Rule Evaluation in the SIEM, and Presentation in the Analyst Triage Queue.
content.subtitle: Tracing Security Telemetry from Host to Analyst Queue

techBox.title: Pipeline Stages
techBox.content:
1. Endpoint Log Generation (Windows EVTX, Sysmon, Linux Syslog)
2. Transport (Universal Forwarder, TCP 9997 / TLS 514)
3. Normalization (Common Information Model field extraction)
4. Correlation (Scheduled SPL/KQL searches trigger on threat logic)
5. Alert Queue (Analyst claims ticket for triage within SLA)

question.text: What are the three core foundational pillars that support any enterprise Security Operations Center?
options: Hardware, Software, Firmware
People, Process, Technology
Firewalls, Antivirus, SIEM
Detection, Response, Recovery
question.explanation: SOC architecture is built upon People (analysts), Process (SOPs and playbooks), and Technology (monitoring tools).

topics.title: Alerts & Events
topics.description: Learn the operational taxonomy separating raw log Events from SIEM Alerts, qualified Incidents, and legal Cases.

content.text: An Event is any observable technical occurrence on a host or network (e.g. user login, packet drop, DHCP lease). An Alert is a signal generated when an event (or sequence of events) satisfies a predefined detection rule or statistical threshold indicating potential threat activity.
content.subtitle: Distinguishing Background Telemetry from Actionable Signals

techBox.title: Volume Reduction Funnel
techBox.content:
• 10,000,000 Events per day (Raw logs, 99.9% benign background noise)
• 1,000 Alerts per day (Rule matches evaluated by Tier 1 analysts)
• 50 Incidents per day (Confirmed malicious threats requiring containment)
• 5 Cases per day (Formal investigation containers tracking remediation & audit evidence)

content.text: An Alert becomes a Security Incident once an analyst investigates and confirms that unauthorized, malicious, or policy-violating activity has occurred. A Case is the formal organizational and legal folder that documents evidence, timeline, actions taken, and post-incident remediation.
content.subtitle: From Technical Confirmation to Legal Chain of Custody

techBox.title: Case Management Requirements
techBox.content:
• Unique Case ID (e.g. INC-2026-042)
• Asset & Identity inventory
• SHA-256 hashes of malware artifacts
• Chronological UTC investigation timeline
• Assigned responder and regulatory notification clock

question.text: Which of the following describes the difference between an Alert and an Incident?
options: Alerts are always false positives, while incidents are always true positives
An alert is an unverified notification triggered by a detection rule; an incident is a confirmed security compromise verified by an analyst
Alerts are created by Tier 3, while incidents are created by Tier 1
There is no difference; the terms are completely interchangeable
question.correctAnswer: An alert is an unverified notification triggered by a detection rule; an incident is a confirmed security compromise verified by an analyst
question.explanation: Alerts are candidate notifications generated by automated rules; an Incident is officially declared only after human verification confirms an active threat or breach.

topics.title: Alert Triage
topics.description: Master systematic alert triage: understand the alert signature, extract core entities (User, Host, IP), verify evidence, and investigate attacks.

units.title: Topic 1: Understand Alert & Identify User, Host & IP

content.text: Alert triage begins by understanding what rule triggered and extracting the core investigation entities: User context (privileges, department, shift), Host context (workstation vs domain controller, asset criticality), and IP context (internal RFC 1918 subnet vs external reputation via AbuseIPDB and VirusTotal).
content.subtitle: The Three Foundational Entities of Security Triage

techBox.title: Entity Extraction Checklist
techBox.content:
1. Alert Rule: MITRE technique, signature logic, trigger threshold
2. User Entity: Account name, domain group, active shift, HR status
3. Host Entity: Hostname, IP address, OS build, business criticality
4. IP Entity: Source vs Destination, internal vs external, Threat Intel reputation

content.text: Verifying evidence requires inspecting process lineage: checking parent-child relationships (e.g. WINWORD.EXE spawning powershell.exe is a high-confidence attack indicator), de-obfuscating Base64 command lines, verifying SHA-256 binary hashes, and checking network flow egress.
content.subtitle: Corroborating Telemetry across Host and Perimeter Sensors

techBox.title: High-Risk Parent-Child Indicators
techBox.content:
• WINWORD.EXE / EXCEL.EXE -> powershell.exe / cmd.exe
• w3wp.exe (IIS Web Server) -> cmd.exe / whoami.exe
• explorer.exe -> rundll32.exe (without command line flags)
• svchost.exe spawned by any parent other than services.exe

question.text: When triaging a process execution alert, why is it critical to examine the parent process (Parent PID/Image)?
options: Parent processes determine the color scheme of the terminal
Legitimate tools like powershell.exe are benign on their own, but being spawned by an Office macro (WINWORD.EXE) reveals an initial access compromise
Parent processes only exist on Linux systems, not Windows
The parent process always runs faster than the child process
question.correctAnswer: Legitimate tools like powershell.exe are benign on their own, but being spawned by an Office macro (WINWORD.EXE) reveals an initial access compromise
question.explanation: Attackers abuse living-off-the-land tools like PowerShell; examining the parent process exposes abnormal execution chains like Office macros spawning shell environments.

topics.title: False Positives
topics.description: Differentiate malicious intrusions from expected administrative activity, benign software behavior, and SIEM detection errors.

content.text: A False Positive (FP) occurs when a detection rule triggers on authorized or benign behavior. Expected Activity includes scheduled IT tasks: vulnerability scanners (Nessus/Qualys), backup jobs (Veeam), software deployment (SCCM/Intune), and approved penetration tests. Benign Behavior includes sysadmins legitimately using administrative utilities (PsExec, certutil, PowerShell).
content.subtitle: Distinguishing Administrative Operations from Adversary Tactics

techBox.title: Verification Techniques for Expected Activity
techBox.content:
• Check Change Management (ServiceNow CHG tickets for maintenance windows)
• Check Asset Classification (Privileged Access Workstations vs standard endpoints)
• Check User Role (Is user an authorized senior sysadmin or a finance clerk?)
• Check Binary Hash (Does binary match authentic Microsoft signed binary?)

units.title: Topic 2: Detection Errors & SIEM Rule Tuning

content.text: Detection Errors happen when SIEM correlation rules are written with overly broad regular expressions or low statistical thresholds. When rules fire indiscriminately, they cause alert fatigue. Tier 1 analysts must report flawed rules to Tier 3 detection engineers with precise narrow exclusions (e.g. filter by known Parent PID, specific signer certificates, or dedicated management subnets).
content.subtitle: The Continuous Feedback Loop Between Triage and Detection Engineering

techBox.title: Tuning Feedback Requirements
techBox.content:
• SIEM Rule ID & Name
• Raw event payload demonstrating false trigger
• Documented business justification (approved IT script)
• Recommended narrow exclusion filter (e.g. ParentImage=CcmExec.exe)

question.text: What is the most reliable way to verify if an alert on administrative tools (e.g. PsExec or Certutil) is expected activity?
options: Ask the user casually over chat if they remember doing it
Cross-reference the activity against approved Change Management tickets (CHG#) and verified maintenance windows
Assume that any action performed by an IT administrator is always safe
Ignore the alert and wait to see if the user complains
question.correctAnswer: Cross-reference the activity against approved Change Management tickets (CHG#) and verified maintenance windows
question.explanation: Authorized administrative actions must correspond to approved Change Management records (ITSM tickets) specifying maintenance windows and designated systems.

topics.title: Severity
topics.description: Classify incident severity (Low, Medium, High, Critical) using asset impact, attacker progress, evidence confidence, and SLA timers.

units.title: Topic 1: Severity Scale: Low, Medium, High & Critical

content.text: Severity defines operational urgency, resource allocation, and response deadlines. Critical (P1) represents enterprise-wide ransomware or domain controller compromise with a 15-minute response SLA. High (P2) covers single-system malware execution or compromised privileged accounts with a 1-hour SLA. Medium (P3) represents isolated suspicious anomalies with a 4-hour SLA. Low (P4) covers minor hygiene and policy violations with a 24-hour SLA.
content.subtitle: Service Level Agreements (SLAs) and Operational Prioritization

techBox.title: SLA Matrix by Severity
techBox.content:
• Critical (P1): 15-min response | 24/7 immediate callout | Active ransomware or DC breach
• High (P2): 1-hour response | Active C2 or compromised privileged account
• Medium (P3): 4-hour response | Isolated suspicious script or unauthorized software
• Low (P4): 24-hour response | Adware, single port scan, minor policy violation

content.text: Severity is mathematically evaluated using the relationship: Severity = Asset Impact × Evidence Confidence. High Impact on a Tier 0 Crown Jewel (Domain Controller, SWIFT Banking Gateway) with High Confidence (EDR process dump + C2 beaconing) produces an immediate Critical rating. Low Confidence signals require rapid validation before disruptive containment.
content.subtitle: Objective Risk Calculation in Security Triage

techBox.title: Scoring Factors
techBox.content:
• Asset Impact: Tier 0 (Crown Jewels: DC, Identity, DB), Tier 1 (Servers), Tier 2 (Endpoints), Tier 3 (Guest Wi-Fi)
• Evidence Confidence: Low (Single heuristic), Medium (Signature match), High (Corroborated multi-sensor IOCs)

question.text: Which of the following incidents represents a Critical (P1) severity level requiring a 15-minute response SLA?
options: A user asking for assistance resetting their Outlook password
Active ransomware encrypting shared drives across multiple enterprise file servers and domain controllers
A marketing employee installing an unauthorized photo editing application
A firewall dropping routine port scan probes from the internet
question.correctAnswer: Active ransomware encrypting shared drives across multiple enterprise file servers and domain controllers
question.explanation: Ransomware actively spreading across core servers and domain controllers causes enterprise-wide operational paralysis and requires immediate P1 Critical response.

topics.title: Escalation
topics.description: Execute seamless incident escalation: tier-to-tier handoffs (L1 → L2, L2 → L3), specialist team engagement, and management briefings.

units.title: Topic 1: Tiered Escalation: L1 → L2 and L2 → L3

content.text: Escalation is the formal transfer of an investigation when technical scope exceeds standard playbooks. Tier 1 escalates to Tier 2 when an alert is verified as a True Positive, requires host memory forensics, or needs complex lateral movement tracking. Tier 2 escalates to Tier 3 when custom malware reverse-engineering, rootkit analysis, or enterprise-wide threat hunting is required.
content.subtitle: Handoff Responsibilities Across the 3-Tier SOC Model

techBox.title: Tier Responsibilities
techBox.content:
• Tier 1 (Triage): Alert intake, IOC extraction, basic containment (host isolation), warm handoff
• Tier 2 (Incident Response): Memory forensics, root cause analysis, lateral movement tracking, eradication
• Tier 3 (Threat Hunter / SME): Binary disassembly, kernel debugging, custom YARA/Sigma creation, threat intel

content.text: Specialist Escalation routes technical requirements to external IT teams: Network Engineering for border firewall blocks and BGP null-routes; IAM Admins for Kerberos Golden Ticket resets (krbtgt rotation). Management Escalation alerts the CISO, Legal, and PR when incidents involve regulatory deadlines (e.g. GDPR 72-hour notification) or executive data.
content.subtitle: Cross-Functional Crisis Coordination and Regulatory Deadlines

techBox.title: Specialist Roles
techBox.content:
• Network Engineers: Edge ACLs, PCAP captures, DNS sinkholes
• IAM / AD Admins: Krbtgt password rotation, enterprise session revocation
• Legal Counsel: Regulatory breach disclosure notices (GDPR, HIPAA, SEC)
• Corporate PR: Unified communications to media and affected customers

question.text: What is a 'warm handoff' during incident escalation, and why is it superior to a 'cold handoff'?
options: A warm handoff requires physically handing a paper file to a manager
A warm handoff involves direct communication with the receiving responder, including a summary of findings, verified IOCs, and actions taken, ensuring zero lost time
A warm handoff can only be done during daylight hours
A cold handoff is always preferred because it avoids talking to colleagues
question.correctAnswer: A warm handoff involves direct communication with the receiving responder, including a summary of findings, verified IOCs, and actions taken, ensuring zero lost time
question.explanation: Warm handoffs transfer full context, containment status, and technical artifacts directly to the receiving responder, preventing duplicate effort and response delays.

topics.title: SOC Documentation
topics.description: Master professional incident documentation: the 5 core pillars (Findings, Evidence, Timeline, Actions, Recommendations), ticketing excellence, and audit readiness.

units.title: Topic 1: The 5 Pillars of Documentation (Findings, Evidence, Timeline, Actions, Recommendation)

content.text: In security operations, 'If it wasn't documented, it never happened.' An audit-grade report contains Five Core Pillars: Findings (executive summary and root cause), Evidence (hashes, IPs, command lines, log snippets), Timeline (second-by-second UTC chronology), Actions (exact containment and remediation steps taken), and Recommendations (strategic preventative controls to stop recurrence).
content.subtitle: The Five Essential Components of Professional Security Records

techBox.title: The Five Pillars of SOC Documentation
techBox.content:
1. Findings: Executive summary, root cause, affected scope
2. Evidence: SHA-256 hashes, C2 IPs/domains, process execution trees
3. Timeline: Chronological sequence of events standardized in ISO 8601 UTC
4. Actions: Containment steps, host isolation, account resets, firewall blocks
5. Recommendations: Hardening advice (GPO restrictions, MFA, rule tuning)

units.title: Topic 2: [Demo] Writing an Effective SOC Ticket

steps.highlight: Transforms an incident into permanent organizational resilience.

demo.conclusion: Professional documentation satisfies auditors, protects the company legally, and hardens enterprise defenses.

question.text: Why must all timestamps in SOC incident documentation be strictly standardized in UTC?
options: UTC looks more professional in email signatures
Enterprises operate across distributed global time zones; standardizing on UTC prevents chronological ambiguity during forensic correlation
UTC prevents hackers from seeing the time of the attack
Security ticketing systems cannot understand local time zones
question.correctAnswer: Enterprises operate across distributed global time zones; standardizing on UTC prevents chronological ambiguity during forensic correlation
question.explanation: Standardizing on UTC eliminates confusion across international assets, remote employees, server logs, and daylight savings transitions.

questions.question: A Tier 1 analyst receives an alert for encoded PowerShell execution spawned by Microsoft Excel on an accounting workstation. Which of the following sequences represents the correct triage and response procedure?
options: Close the alert as expected financial activity without checking process arguments
Reboot the workstation immediately, delete the Excel file, and email the user
Understand the alert rule, extract User/Host/IP entities, inspect parent-child process lineage, de-obfuscate arguments, and isolate the host upon confirming malicious C2 download
Escalate immediately to the CEO without documenting technical findings or isolating the host
questions.explanation: Methodical triage requires understanding detection logic, extracting entities, decoding script arguments, verifying evidence, and applying immediate containment (host isolation) before escalating.

questions.question: During shift review, an analyst discovers that scheduled vulnerability scans by the internal Nessus scanner (10.0.99.10) generate 1,500 port scan alerts every Wednesday night. How should this be handled?
options: Block the Nessus scanner IP address at the internal firewall
Turn off all firewall alerting permanently
Document the authorized change ticket, resolve current alerts as False Positives (Expected Activity), and submit a rule tuning ticket to exclude the scanner IP from port scan alerting
Escalate to Tier 3 as an ongoing distributed denial of service attack
questions.explanation: Authorized vulnerability scanning is expected administrative activity. Documenting the change record and submitting a SIEM tuning ticket eliminates noise without creating blind spots.

questions.question: An active ransomware intrusion is detected actively encrypting shared volumes across the enterprise Primary Domain Controller (DC-01). What severity rating must be assigned, and what is the typical SLA response timeframe?
options: Low (P4) with a 24-hour response SLA
Medium (P3) with a 4-hour response SLA
Critical (P1) with a 15-minute response SLA, 24/7 emergency bridge activation, and executive leadership notification
Informational (P5) with no response required
questions.explanation: Ransomware actively compromising domain controllers threatens enterprise survival; it is classified as Critical (P1) with a mandatory 15-minute response SLA.

questions.question: When handing off an ongoing, contained incident from Tier 1 to Tier 2 (L1 → L2 Escalation), what must be included in the 'warm handoff' package?
options: Just the alert ID and the word 'help'
Executive findings, affected User/Host/IP entities, verified technical IOCs (hashes/C2 IPs), chronological UTC timeline, proof of host containment, and direct notification to the responder
The analyst personal cell phone number only
A request to close the ticket immediately
questions.explanation: A warm handoff provides structured findings, verified IOCs, timeline, and containment proof so Tier 2 can immediately begin deep forensics without re-triaging.

questions.question: What are the Five Core Pillars of professional SOC incident documentation that ensure audit and regulatory compliance?
options: Findings, Evidence, Timeline, Actions, Recommendations
Introduction, Hypothesis, Experiment, Results, Conclusion
User ID, Password, Hash, IP, Port
Firewall, SIEM, EDR, SOAR, NDR
questions.explanation: Audit-proof incident documentation requires Findings (summary), Evidence (technical IOCs), Timeline (chronology in UTC), Actions (containment steps), and Recommendations (preventative hardening).
